title: Acute cholangitis: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 diagnosis, grading and drainage timing

guidelineVersions: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18): diagnostic criteria and severity grading (Kiriyama et al., J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2018)
Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18): initial management and flowchart (Miura et al., J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2018)
NICE QS104: Gallstone disease quality standard (published 3 December 2015)

related.why: Pathology of gallstones and cholecystitis, a leading cause of biliary obstruction underlying cholangitis
Applied anatomy of Calot's triangle and the biliary tree relevant to the site of obstruction
Acute cholecystitis: a related but distinct biliary emergency with its own TG18 grading and timing

brief.scenario: Mrs Ruth Calloway, 72, has had 2 days of fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. She has known gallstones. She is confused, HR 118, BP 95/60, temperature 39.2°C.
brief.task: Diagnose the condition, apply the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 diagnostic criteria and severity grading, and outline immediate management including biliary drainage timing.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Work through TG18 systematically: confirm the diagnosis (A + B/C), grade the severity, then let the grade set the urgency of drainage.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating this as straightforward sepsis without naming organ dysfunction, which is what actually makes it Grade III and changes the drainage timeline.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is acute cholangitis with sepsis; I want to apply the Tokyo Guidelines criteria and grade her severity."

flow: Apply the TG18 diagnostic criteria (A, B, C)

grid.label: Diagnosis and TG18 criteria (A/B/C)
grid.fail: Does not name acute cholangitis, or cannot structure the diagnosis around systemic inflammation, cholestasis and imaging.
grid.pass: Diagnoses acute cholangitis via TG18: A (systemic inflammation — fever, abnormal WBC/CRP), B (cholestasis — jaundice, deranged LFTs), C (imaging — duct dilation/cause); definite diagnosis needs all three.
grid.high: Distinguishes TG18 suspected diagnosis (A plus B or C) from definite (A+B+C); notes TG18 has no separate criterion for prior biliary disease — it supports, not completes, the diagnosis.

grid.label: Severity grading
grid.fail: Does not grade severity, or grades using vague terms ("looks septic") rather than the TG18 criteria.
grid.pass: Grade III: any one new dysfunction (vasopressors, altered consciousness, PaO2/FiO2<300, oliguria/creatinine>2.0 mg/dL, INR>1.5, platelets<100,000/mm³). Grade II: two of WBC>12,000 or <4,000/μL, temp≥39°C, age≥75, bilirubin≥5 mg/dL, albumin<25 g/L. Grade I: neither.
grid.high: Correctly grades this patient as III on confusion (neurological dysfunction) and hypotension, and states severity should be reassessed through the admission as it can change.

grid.label: Immediate resuscitation and antibiotics
grid.fail: Delays antibiotics or fluid resuscitation, or treats this as a purely biliary problem without sepsis management.
grid.pass: Manages as sepsis: cultures before antibiotics if this doesn't delay treatment, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (gram-negative/anaerobic cover) within the hour, IV fluids, oxygen, and monitoring lactate/urine output.
grid.high: Names a specific regimen appropriate to severity (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem for a Grade III/biliary-sepsis presentation) and adds vasopressor support if hypotension persists despite fluids.

grid.label: Escalation for Grade III disease
grid.fail: Manages Grade III cholangitis on a general ward without escalation.
grid.pass: States Grade III cholangitis needs critical care (ICU/HDU) referral alongside organ support.
grid.high: Explains escalation should happen in parallel with resuscitation and drainage planning, not sequentially after either.

grid.label: Biliary drainage timing by grade
grid.fail: Applies the same drainage timeframe regardless of grade, or delays drainage in Grade III disease pending full recovery.
grid.pass: States drainage follows severity: Grade III needs urgent drainage once stable; Grade II needs early drainage, commonly within 24–48h; Grade I is antibiotics first, drainage reserved for non-response.
grid.high: States ERCP is first-line, PTBD the alternative if ERCP fails/unavailable, and NICE QS104 sets a 24-hour target for emergency ERCP if not responding to antibiotics/fluids.

grid.label: Safety-critical: recognising severe disease behind a reassuring history
grid.fail: Assumes the absence of a full Charcot's triad excludes cholangitis, or is reassured because no single feature is dramatic.
grid.pass: States the complete Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) is present in only a minority of contemporary cases, so its absence doesn't exclude the diagnosis.
grid.high: Adds that Reynolds' pentad (triad plus hypotension and altered mental status) marks severe disease, and mortality is substantially higher with bacteraemia or shock than uncomplicated cases.

high.text: What's the diagnosis, and how would you confirm it?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Acute cholangitis with sepsis. TG18 needs A — systemic inflammation — plus B or C for a suspected diagnosis, or all three for a definite one; her known gallstones support the picture but aren't themselves one of the A/B/C criteria.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Grade III on confusion and hypotension — either alone is enough, since Grade III only needs dysfunction in one system. I'd keep reassessing the grade through her admission, since it can worsen.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Sepsis Six with blood cultures before antibiotics where that doesn't delay treatment, broad-spectrum cover such as piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem, IV fluids, and vasopressor support if she stays hypotensive.

failures.move: Calling the case "severe" without applying the TG18 grading criteria.
failures.consequence: Grade drives the urgency of drainage; an ungraded judgement risks under- or over-treating.

failures.move: Delaying antibiotics to wait for further results.
failures.consequence: Delayed source control and antibiotics in biliary sepsis increases the risk of deterioration and death.

failures.move: Managing Grade III cholangitis without critical care involvement.
failures.consequence: Organ support is delayed in a patient who may need vasopressors or higher-level monitoring.

failures.move: Waiting for full recovery before considering biliary drainage.
failures.consequence: The underlying obstruction persists, risking ongoing or recurrent sepsis and organ dysfunction.

failures.move: Excluding cholangitis because the classic triad is incomplete.
failures.consequence: A real, potentially severe case is missed because most patients never have all three classic features together.

recovery.when: You're not sure which grade applies
recovery.line: Let me check systematically: is there organ dysfunction anywhere? If not, does she meet two of the five Grade II criteria?

recovery.when: Asked whether imaging is essential before treating
recovery.line: I wouldn't delay antibiotics or resuscitation for imaging, but I would still arrange it to confirm criterion C and plan drainage.

knowledge.fact: TG18 definite diagnosis needs one item from each of A (systemic inflammation), B (cholestasis) and C (imaging); suspected diagnosis needs A plus B or C. There is no separate criterion for prior biliary disease.
TG18 Grade II (moderate) needs two of: WBC >12,000 or <4,000/μL, temperature ≥39°C, age ≥75, bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL, albumin <25 g/L.
TG18 Grade III (severe) is new dysfunction in any one organ system (cardiovascular, neurological, respiratory, renal, hepatic or haematological).

TG18 links drainage urgency to grade: Grade III needs urgent/emergency drainage once fit for the procedure; Grade II needs early drainage, commonly within 24–48 hours; Grade I is treated with antibiotics first, drainage reserved for non-response.

NICE's gallstone quality standard states adults with common bile duct stones needing emergency ERCP should have it within 24 hours, for cholangitis/pancreatitis not responding to antibiotics or IV fluids.
The complete Charcot's triad (jaundice, fever, RUQ pain) is reported in only a minority of acute cholangitis patients, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.

recall.think: Could this progress to organ failure? Does grade set drainage urgency?
recall.say: "Acute cholangitis — Tokyo Guidelines set severity grade and drainage timeline."
do: Diagnose via TG18 A/B/C; grade I–III
Sepsis Six: cultures, antibiotics within the hour, fluids, oxygen, lactate/urine output
Match drainage urgency to grade; escalate Grade III urgently

numbers.meaning: any one organ dysfunction → urgent/emergency drainage once stable
target for emergency ERCP if not responding to antibiotics/fluids

recall.trap: Absent Charcot's triad doesn't exclude cholangitis — most patients lack all three features.
recall.finish: ERCP first-line for drainage (PTBD if unavailable); cholecystectomy once recovered, for gallstone cause.

partner.opening: Present the scenario: Mrs Calloway, 72, fever, RUQ pain, jaundice, confused, HR 118, BP 95/60, temp 39.2°C. "What's your diagnosis and how would you confirm it?"

reveals.finding: WBC 16.2, CRP 210, bilirubin 68 µmol/L, ALP and GGT markedly raised, albumin 22 g/L.
Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a stone at the distal end.
GCS 13 (confused), lactate 3.2, requiring a fluid bolus to maintain blood pressure.

push.question: What if ERCP isn't available at your centre?
push.expect: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage as the alternative, with transfer considered if neither is available locally.

push.question: What if she were Grade I instead?
push.expect: Antibiotics first-line, with drainage reserved for those who don't respond.

push.question: What's the definitive treatment once she recovers?
push.expect: Cholecystectomy for gallstone aetiology once she has recovered from the acute episode.

curveballs.prompt: She has a biliary stent in situ from a previous ERCP.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider stent occlusion as the likely cause; the same TG18 diagnosis, grading and management principles still apply.

curveballs.prompt: Her blood pressure doesn't improve despite two fluid boluses.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Start vasopressor support and escalate urgently to critical care; this confirms Grade III disease.

curveballs.prompt: A junior colleague says she can't have cholangitis because she isn't in pain.
curveballs.safeAnswer: The full triad, including pain, is absent in many patients; her fever, jaundice and imaging findings are enough to proceed.

curveballs.prompt: The on-call endoscopist says ERCP can't happen for 72 hours.
curveballs.safeAnswer: For Grade III disease this delay isn't acceptable; escalate for urgent transfer to a centre that can drain her sooner, or arrange percutaneous drainage.
